entries.title: Focus group invites sent to White Sox fans as part of Justin Isbhia's South Loop stadium proposal
entries.summary: <p>Some White Sox fans received an interesting email on Friday afternoon.</p><p>The message invoked public reports of “future White Sox owner Justin Ishbia’s vision for a new, state-of-the-art ballpark,” and invited fans to RSVP for “a limited number of in-person focus group sessions” early next month to give feedback on “potential ballpark features, seating experiences, and overall game-day enhancements” for the proposed new stadium.</p><p>The emails also had a White Sox logo at the top, and all the legal language of an MLB-approved message at the bottom.</p><p>But despite the appearances, the Sox indicate they are just acting as mailmen. The focus groups are being held by Ishbia’s City River Holdings venture, which has been working to develop <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/10/28/bridgeport-bears-domed-stadium-proposal-sox-rate-field" target="_blank" ><u>a mixed-use district in the South Loop with the proposed title of “The Railyards”</u></a> that will house a new White Sox stadium. Rather than hand over customer contact info to a third party, the team is assisting by sending the emails themselves.</p><p>“When we announced the vision for The Railyards in September, we said this was the beginning of a multi-year planning and approval process, and this is part of that process,” a spokesperson for Ishbia explained in an email.</p><p>The feedback received from these groups could affect future stadium proposals, or be used to demonstrate the public support level for the project.</p><p>These invites hit the inboxes of Sox fans at the end of a week that brought word of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/26/amtraks-bridgeport-railyard-to-get-environmental-review-after-community-pressure-lets-keep-up-the-fight" target="_blank" ><u>Amtrak’s proposed new facility in Bridgeport undergoing a federal environmental review</u></a>, after months of pressure from neighborhood residents. The proposal is a corresponding effort with Ishbia’s plans to develop the site of Amtrak’s current facility into the Sox’ future home. The team’s current lease with Bridgeport’s Rate Field runs through the 2029 season, which is also the first year that Ishbia’s ownership transfer agreement with current chairman Jerry Reinsdorf could see the former take control of the franchise.</p><p>Until then, all White Sox business is to remain under the current chairman’s purview. As such, it would have been surprising to see the club sending out official emails embracing Ishbia’s future plans. Instead, everyone involved says the Sox are just acting as the messenger.</p>

entries.title: New faces at new places in high school boys basketball
entries.summary: <p>There wasn’t a whole lot of turnover in the basketball coaching carousel this past offseason. But there were a few intriguing spots to be filled.</p><p>Here is a closer look at several new coaches who will be leading six of the bigger programs in the area this season.</p><p>Glenbard North<br><b>Former coach: </b>Kevin Tonn<br><b>New coach: </b>Nick Healy</p><p>After leading the Panthers to 24 wins and DuKane Conference and regional championships, Tonn felt the pull of his alma mater and took the Wheaton North job.</p><p>Now Healy, the son of Wheaton South head coach Mike Healy and most recently an assistant at Waubonsie Valley, takes over a team that could be ranked in the preseason with four returning starters. That strong nucleus includes the talented 1-2 punch of 6-3 Lamari Carpenter and 6-6 Oturo Redento.</p><p>Lake Park<br><b>Former coach: </b>Billy Pitcher<br><b>New coach: </b>Bob Reibel</p><p>Reibel crosses over from coaching Lake Park’s girls program, where he won both DuKane Conference and regional titles while setting a program record for wins, to lead the boys. He has been the girls coach for the last three seasons.</p><p>Reibel inherits some exciting players, including 6-6 Brennan Shannon and sophomores Christian Burge and Frank Battaglia.</p><p>Oswego East<br><b>Former coach: </b>Ryan Velasquez<br><b>New coach: </b>Brian Johnson</p><p>Oswego East basketball enjoyed a terrific nine-year run under Velasquez, who stepped down after going 198-71 and winning 20-plus games every season except for the Covid-shortened one.</p><p>The search for a coach landed on one with experience. Johnson led West Aurora for eight years and Kaneland for six. Johnson, who most recently was an assistant coach at Metea Valley, won four regionals and a sectional title in 2018 while at West Aurora.</p><p>St. Viator<br><b>Former coach: </b>Michael O’Keefe<br><b>New coach: </b>Al Biancalana</p><p>There isn’t a new coach with more experience than Biancalana.</p><p>The veteran coach has 25 years of head-coaching experience, including stints at Glenbard East, DeKalb, York and Stagg. He also was a Division I assistant at Bradley and UIC for 10 years. Most recently, Biancalana has spent the last four years as Mike Bailey’s assistant at St. Patrick.</p><p>While there were departures and turnover in the program, Biancalana does have veteran returner Dawson Charles to build around in Year 1. He averaged 19.2 points last season as a junior.</p><p>Cary-Grove<br><b>Former coach: </b>Adam McCloud<br><b>New coach: </b>Christian Spandiary</p><p>There were a couple of highs over McCloud’s 10-year run as coach, including last year’s conference championship team that won 28 games. The 2019-20 season produced a school-record 31 wins and a regional title.</p><p>Now Spandiary takes over. As a former star player at Schaumburg and assistant coach at Barrington, Spandiary brings his Mid-Suburban League roots to the Fox Valley Conference. He takes over a team that lost all five starters.</p><p>Schaumburg<br><b>Former coach: </b>Jason Tucker<br><b>New coach: </b>Garett Gatz</p><p>Gatz takes over a program after five years as an assistant, including the last four as the sophomore coach. Before his time at Schaum-<br>burg, Gatz worked under highly successful Conant coach Tom McCormack, now retired, who he also played for in high school.</p><p>The Saxons, who have very little returning from a year ago, have just one regional championship in the last 14 years.</p>

entries.title: Patrick Williams' contract status carries no weight with Bulls regime
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – The groin injury that sidelined Patrick Williams the last week was in the past. His days of being a continual DNP (Did Not Play) Coach’s Decision were not.</p><p>That doesn’t mean Bulls coach Tiago Splitter doesn’t see value in the No. 4 overall pick from the 2020 draft, letting him know to stay ready. Staying ready, however, and seeing playing time as a rotation piece are two very different conversations.</p><p>“I told him during the whole camp and before we started the games he was doing a great job, he was forcing his hand and making my life difficult because he was doing a good job,” Splitter said on Friday. “He’s got to stay ready. His moment is going to come. You can’t just switch rotations every day. You’ve got to stick to something and evaluate, see how the young guys are doing. He’s going to have time to play and there will be changes made throughout the season, so he’s ready to go.”</p><p>Unfortunately for Williams there’s a handful of players in front of him that are not only ready to go but have proven more with this new coaching staff. Rookie Caleb Wilson and Matas Buzelis are the starting forwards, while Isaac Okoro, Leonard Miller and Noa Essengue are the backup forwards Splitter has been using.</p><p>That line Williams is waiting in is only about to get longer when Nic Claxton (hamstring) is able to make his Bulls debut. That means Jalen Smith becomes the back-up five/four, adding to the logjam in the frontcourt.</p><p>And yes, Williams might be the highest paid of all that group at $18 million a year through the 2028-29 season in which he will undoubtedly pick up his player option, but that has no influence with the new front office or coaching staff.</p><p>Splitter was asked if there had been any conversations with executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham in which the coach was told that Williams had to be looked at for minutes just because of the contract he was carrying, and Splitter replied, “No, we never had that conversation.”</p><p></p><p><b>Crafty veteran</b></p><p></p><p>Okoro doesn’t need to be reminded that he is in the final year of a deal in which he makes $11.8 million this season, admitting that it’s not something that weighs on his mind or influences the way he takes the court each night.</p><p>Yes, he can be a valuable trade asset come February if the front office wants to move him but his mindset was that’s a concern for another day.</p><p>“It’s my seventh year in the league,” Okoro said. “I know what comes with it. I know every time I step on the court I’ve got to play my game. I have to do what I do best. There’s no, ‘Oh it’s a contract year so I’ve got to go out and shoot 10 threes a game, I’ve got to be ball dominant.’ Like no, I’ve been in the league this long being who I’ve been. So anytime I step on the court it’s about playing hard, being competitive, try and lead the team the way I can. You got to focus on the Chicago Bulls and how can we get wins, how can we get better.”</p><p></p><p><b>Training room</b></p><p></p><p>Rookie Dailyn Swain was unavailable against Boston, dealing with soreness, according to Splitter.</p><p>“We decided to not have him playing, nothing serious,” Splitter said of Swain, who was not in the rotation mix anyway this season.</p><p>Claxton continued ramping up his activity during the morning shootaround and the hope remained getting him in practices on this current road trip.</p>

entries.title: Lake View hospital kitchen reopens after license pulled for 'cockroach infestation,' other violations
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Masonic Medical Center's cafeteria and kitchen has reopened after it was shuttered earlier this month when a “cockroach infestation” contributed to a failed health inspection, according to the Chicago Department of Public Health.</p><p>The kitchen had its license suspended Oct. 16 for failing the inspection, and multiple citations were issued, but it was reinstated Thursday after a follow-up inspection, the department said in a statement Friday.</p><p>In the report published earlier this month, city inspectors said they observed more than 200 live cockroaches in multiple areas, which included food preparation areas, the grill and deep fryer areas, dry storage and the main dish room, per <a class="Link" href="https://data.cityofchicago.org/Health-Human-Services/Food-Inspections/4ijn-s7e5/data_preview" target="_blank" ><u>city records</u></a>. Dead roaches were found under the dry storage racks for a second time after staff were instructed to clean them during an inspection earlier this year.</p><p>It also detailed black slime accumulating inside a cooler until it dripped onto ice being used for the cafeterias. Inspectors also observed utensils being improperly stored, old food on walls and a mounted can opener. There were leaky pipes and accumulations of dust, grease, and dirt throughout the kitchen and storage areas. </p><p>Other previous violations were also said to have not been corrected.</p><p>The follow-up inspection shows the hospital had exterminators at the premises and remedied all other violations, according to city documents. Advocate Health, which operates Illinois Masonic, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The Rendezvous Cafeteria and patient kitchen at the hospital passed an inspection with conditions April 15. City officials noted the dead cockroaches in the dry storage area and said the kitchens were storing raw chicken above 56 degrees and other foods at similarly high temperatures. A manager, the inspection said, disposed of $250 in food on the spot, though citations were still issued.</p><p>The hospital’s Ecos Cafe also faced citations for storing food at high temperatures and having the handwashing sink in its prep area obstructed by clutter, among other issues, per a separate April 15 report. In that case, employees disposed of nine pounds of food that inspectors had marked as improperly stored.</p><p>It's the fifth time since 2010 that a kitchen at the hospital has failed a health inspection, per city records.</p><p>The hospital last failed a city inspection in August 2023, when inspectors once noted the buildup of black slime in the ice machines and on food — such as salmon and chicken — being stored at improperly high temperatures, per the report.</p>

entries.title: Inspired by Frank Lloyd Wright then wronged by neglect, South Park Terrace heads for auction
entries.summary: <p>A picturesque 121-year-old South Side courtyard building inspired by an historic Frank Lloyd Wright design — and featured in a 1995 Halle Berry movie — is now scheduled for auction.</p><p>South Park Terrace, a Prairie School-styled apartment building at 6116 S. King Drive, is set to be auctioned off Nov. 16-18, according to a marketing brochure by Frontline Real Estate Partners.</p><p>The opening bid is $100,000. </p><p>"We do expect it to go for significantly more than that," Frontline Principal Matthew Tarshis said.</p><p>Frontline was named South Park Terrace's court-appointed receiver, after the building was vacated under city order in 2025 due to its dilapidated condition.</p><p>Officials saw the situation as exigent enough that residents had to begin leaving the building with just two days notice.</p><p>The city’s Department of Buildings said in a statement at the time that the owners, listed then as Brooklyn, New York’s 6116 MLK, “completely abandoned the building, allowing the property to go into foreclosure, and King Dr. is boarded up after tenants were told in 2025 to vacate the premises.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Frontline's 14-page marketing brochure touts the location of the two-story, 52-unit Washington Park building and its notable, park-like private courtyard.</p><p>South Park Terrace is on a major public transit route, is two blocks from a CTA Green Line stop and near the jobs-rich University of Chicago and medical complex.</p><p>Preservation Chicago placed South Park Terrace on its 2026 list of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/03/04/art-institute-expansion-louis-sullivan-chicago-stock-exchange" >Chicago’s seven most endangered places</a>, but there's cause for relief: The building is not being marketed as a tear-down.</p><p>"We believe that the highest and best use for the property is for somebody to come in, and hopefully inject fresh capital, renovate the property, and ideally lease it up and stabilize it," Tarshis said.</p><p>Me too.</p><p>What a great building. And its close to the Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvery Vaux-designed Washington Park and near more amenities and employment opportunities than you can shake a stick at.</p><p>And shame on every entity — public and private — that let such well-designed, affordably priced housing fall into ruin. If any building deserves a second chance, it’s this one.</p><p>Built in 1905 for developer Thomas E. entries.title: Eshun Flowers' punt-block TD sparks Simeon to a 6A playoff win over Oak Lawn
entries.summary: <p>Simeon's youngsters had to grow up in a hurry, and they did.</p><p>The Wolverines ran a gauntlet of tough teams to open the season, losing their first three games and five of their first six. But Simeon survived and has won five in a row, the latest 28-19 over host Oak Lawn Friday night in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class6a-illinois-2026" >Class 6A</a> first round.</p><p>"We had everybody putting us down, just giving up on us," sophomore quarterback Aki King said. "We ain't give up on ourselves. That was the main thing. We just went out there, kept fighting."</p><p>They did it once more against Oak Lawn, rallying from a 13-6 deficit with three straight scores.</p><p>The last came on the first play of the fourth quarter when sophomore Eshun Flowers blocked a Spartans punt, scooped it up and ran 25 yards for a touchdown to give Simeon (6-5) a 28-13 lead.</p><p>"Oh, that was wonderful," said Simeon junior Bryce Kidd, who ran for one TD and caught a pass for another. "That was the game-sealer, right there."</p><p>Earlier, King threw a 25-yard TD pass to Kidd and Kidd raced 79 yards down the right sideline for another score.</p><p>Running back James Bell, one of the state's top uncommitted seniors, added an eight-yard TD run for the Wolverines, who play next week against Nazareth or Dunlap.</p><p>King ran seven times for 55 yards and was 4-of-9 passing for 57 yards as Oak Lawn (7-3) built its defensive game plan around containing the pass-and-catch duo of King and fellow soph Jalonny Billingsley.</p><p>"That's why we try to use our tendencies to our advantage in certain situations and whatnot, knowing that J5 [Billingsley] is going to get a lot of attention," Simeon coach Sinque Turner said. "And we've got a kid that's a track star [Kidd] that we can get the ball to, and he can make some of the same [or] similar plays as Jalonny."</p><p>King, meanwhile, has grown into his role after those early losses.</p><p>"Just by him going through the things he's been going through over these last 12, 11 games or whatnot, he's gained a lot of experience against a lot of top competition," Turner said. "So he's matured drastically. ... Still a lot of growing to do, but nonetheless, I think the sky's the limit for that kid."</p><p>King is seeing the reward for the work he put in over the offseason, with Kidd and the rest of his receivers.</p><p>"We've been [doing] seven-on-seven with each other for a year and some change now," King said. "[Kidd is] just a dog, track style. He gets in. the open field, he ain't getting caught."</p><p>After Flowers' touchdown, Simeon's defense stepped up with a pair of fumble recoveries and a fourth-down stop at its own two-yard line. entries.title: Little-known Goode entertains the state in 88-84 playoff loss to Quincy played at two different fields
entries.summary: <p>Goode is one of the newer high schools in Chicago. It opened in 2012 and started up a football program in 2014. Few people have even heard of the school. Until Friday. </p><p>Goode played an astounding Class 6A state playoff game against visiting Quincy. The Knights lost 88-84 in a game that started at 3 p.m., lasted four hours, set multiple state records, and had to be moved to a second high school when darkness set in. Goode's field does not have lights. </p><p>“Survive and advance. I am proud to say we did that tonight,” Quincy coach Rick Little told the WGEM streaming broadcast following the game. “I am proud of this team and their resolve.”</p><p>Chicago Public Schools scheduled the game for 3 p.m. on Saturday at Rockne Stadium. But since Quincy didn't have school on Friday they asked Goode if the teams could play the game on Friday afternoon. Goode agreed. </p><p>The fireworks arrived as soon as the game started and Goode led 60-59 at halftime. The halftime break was shortened to six minutes. Officials were worried about the impending darkness. </p><p>The game was suspended at 5:50 p.m. with Quincy ahead 88-84 and 3:42 left to play. Everyone headed over to Englewood high school to finish the game. </p><p>Play restarted at 6:53 p.m. </p><p>Quincy quarterback Bryson Little threw a state single-game record eight touchdown passes and rushed for two TDs.</p><p>The combined 172 points are the most-ever in a high school game in Illinois, topping the 166 set scored when Springfield beat Rock Island 94-72 on October 29, 2021.</p><p>“This is why we love high school sports,” IHSA Executive Director Craig Anderson said. “The circumstances weren’t ideal, but everyone involved came together on behalf of students, and the result is something that no one involved with this game is ever going to forget. I encourage anyone reading this to go support a local high school event this weekend. Whether it is another football playoff game, a Sectional Championship soccer match, or a Sectional Cross Country meet. You may not see as many records fall as you did in the Quincy-Goode game, but what you will see is the epitome of education-based athletics: young people giving everything they have while representing their schools and communities.”<br></p>

entries.title: Intense, underrated Oklahoma State recruit TJ Lewis powers Bolingbrook past Lockport
entries.summary: <p>Bolingbrook senior TJ Lewis runs so hard in practice that his coach, Titcus Pettigrew, worries it might get dangerous.</p><p>‘‘We have to take him out sometimes,’’ Pettigrew said. ‘‘The intensity. And the defense doesn’t let up. Someone is going to injure someone with how hard he runs and how hard they hit. It is just his passion. He has a big chip on his shoulder. And he has some big shoulders.’’</p><p>Lewis says that chip on his shoulder is because national recruiting websites have underrated him.</p><p>‘‘I’m ranked No. 32 in Illinois right now [by 247Sports.com], which is not true,’’ Lewis said. ‘‘They can see it like that. entries.title: Rookie Caleb Wilson blasts Bulls, self after blowout loss in Boston
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – There was actually a hint of enthusiasm in Josh Giddey’s voice.</p><p>The Bulls guard was standing in the visiting locker room of Boston’s TD Garden on Monday, discussing the pending rematch just a few days later.</p><p>“We get another chance at these guys so it will be good to see how we respond,” Giddey insisted after that 134-99 drubbing.</p><p>Response seen.</p><p>Everyone, cover your eyes.</p><p>For the second time in a five-day period, the rebuilding Bulls (1-5) strolled into TD Garden with high hopes only to see them thrown to the ground, stomped on and discarded with the other trash left on the court. It was another uncompetitive night against the Celtics, a 125-111 romp. And the first game of pool play in the NBA Cup wasn’t even that close.</p><p>Rookie Caleb Wilson called out everything, including the effort and himself.</p><p>“I’m 20, and I’ve never been a loser in my whole life, so I’m going to try my best to make sure that doesn’t happen, and I’m not ever going to accept being a loser,” Wilson said of trying to will the team back into it in the second half. “This is my job, to be a leader on this team, and it’s all going to start with me. I know that. It’s partially my fault that we started off the way we did, whether I’m the youngest on the team or not. I take ownership for that, and it won’t happen again.”</p><p>Boston (4-1) put on a clinic in every facet of the game from the opening tip Friday, outscoring the Bulls 44-25 in the first quarter.</p><p>The Celtics outscored the Bulls 24-10 in the paint and outshot them 67% to 32% from the field, and their bench put up 22 points compared to the Bulls second unit’s measly four in the first quarter.</p><p>It was disappointing, considering the Bulls were looking forward to seeing how they would respond against a top-tier team in the East, but even more so because they had just played one of their better games Wednesday against the defending NBA champion Knicks.</p><p>Lesson learned: Momentum in a rebuild is just a three-syllable word.</p><p>“I know our team doesn’t have superstars like Jayson Tatum and Paul George, but we’re young, and that’s going to be our advantage all year,” Wilson said. “If we’re not going to play hard, it’s not going to work. We’re going to lose every game. We’re all young; we shouldn’t be letting anyone play harder than us.”</p><p>Wilson wasn’t the only one who had something to say after a second-half play in which Payton Pritchard snatched a rebound from Matas Buzelis, knocking him to the ground, then seconds later took advantage of a Bulls turnover with a three-pointer. Buddy Hield was vocal on the bench with his teammates during the timeout.</p><p>“Buddy was just saying that we needed to have some type of pride and passion, and I agree with it, for sure,” Wilson said. “I mean, we’re the Chicago Bulls. I feel like it’s unacceptable to be looking like we are and also be laying down that early in the game.”</p><p>Wilson had 23 points, including six three-pointers, five rebounds and four assists.</p><p>But the game was disappointing overall, especially defensively, where it looked like strides were being made.</p><p>“My motto is always day-by-day,” Isaac Okoro said of the defense. “I can see us starting to be more physical, picking up full court, getting into the ball more as the game goes on because everybody is preaching it just more and more. That doesn’t mean it’s where it needs to be at all.”</p>

entries.title: Eyes on Bears deal, data center regulation bill
entries.summary: <p>A few weeks ago, Gov. JB Pritzker told reporters that negotiators are closer than they’d ever been to a deal with the Bears to stay in Illinois. The Bears are threatening to decamp to a wasteland in Northwest Indiana’s dirty energy and industrial corridor.</p><p>As you’ve probably read before, Illinois’ offer is to create a privately funded local sports stadium authority to build and operate a new stadium which would be surrounded by an entertainment complex. The state would still be on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars in public infrastructure spending for the Bears-owned Arlington Heights site, and nobody knows how much that could be if the Bears decide to stay somewhere in Chicago.</p><p>As of this writing, the Bears have not committed to anything. The Legislature and governor, understandably, don’t want to pass a bill and still watch the Bears leave, so until the Bears give the go-ahead nothing will happen.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2e0000" name="module-2e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>But other major issues have been vying for attention during the mid-to-late November veto session. One of the major proposals is legislation to put some hardened guardrails around the construction and operation of new data centers.</p><p>My associate Isabel Miller and I came up with a question to ask Pritzker last week to see if we could gauge what he thinks about the current data center situation: Is the data center regulation bill just as close to passage this fall as the Bears bill?</p><p>I’d heard that the Senate was hoping to hammer it out, but that the House was intending to shift the proposal, along with a new clean energy bill, to a special January "lame duck” session before the new General Assembly is sworn in, for a possible solution.</p><p>“I don't know how to measure whether it's just as close,” Pritzker said about the data center bill, and then reverted back to discussing the Bears bill. “I can tell you this: that there's a lot of work that's being done even as we speak on that Bears bill, so I'm very hopeful that in the second week of veto session there might be a vote on it.”</p><p>In other words, maybe in January. Maybe.</p><p>Data centers are a tricky issue for Democrats because organized labor wants to build more of them and pretty much everyone else in the state doesn’t want anything to do with them, including environmentalists, who worry the companies will try to use new carbon-based energy to operate them.</p><p>But the reality is, new gas-powered plants probably wouldn’t be economically feasible as long as those plants must be closed under existing state law by 2040. It takes years and years to build new gas generators these days. By the time a new plant was actually up and running and serving a data center, it would have just a few years to generate revenue before shutting down. That’s not enough time to pay off the debt. And almost nobody sees any way that Illinois will significantly relax its deadline, especially since commercial solar and wind power sources tied to battery storage have become cheaper to build and deploy.</p><p>Pritzker has issued a one-year pause on tax breaks for new data centers but that won’t solve anything.</p><p>The really big data centers that are making headlines everywhere likely won’t ever be built here. Our state’s Biometric Information Privacy Act has very stiff penalties for storing images of people online without their knowledge or consent. Those data centers are being built as part of the massive artificial intelligence expansion that appears to be in a huge financial bubble right now. It would just be far too costly to fend off the lawsuits to keep those centers open.</p><p>Then there are other hugely important data center issues like water usage and driving up existing energy prices.</p><p>People are freaked out about these data centers, and it’s only natural. Ever since humans evolved, they’ve guarded their fire and water sources with their lives. They are two basic elements of life.</p><p>And now these massive, faceless companies are wanting to snatch up our electricity and water, all while warning everyone who will listen that their technology will likely wipe out humankind.</p><p>They’re behaving like monsters and ogres from folk tales handed down from time immemorial. And the public is rightly having none of it.</p><p>So, maybe a few weeks after the Democrats likely score major state and national wins by railing against the “forces of evil” might not be a great time to publicly give a billionaire football team a catered deal while walking away from the nation’s chief economic ogres.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-650000" name="module-650000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Narrative of cities failing under Black leadership are stereotypical, untrue
entries.summary: <p>For years, Americans have been told a familiar story.</p><p>Major cities led by Black elected officials are supposedly synonymous with crime, disorder and decline. From campaign rallies to cable television appearances, political leaders have repeatedly invoked Chicago, Baltimore, Atlanta, Newark and other cities as cautionary tales. The message has been unmistakable: Black leadership has failed, and urban America is spiraling out of control.</p><p>The facts tell a different story.</p><p>Across the country, violent crime is falling. Homicides declined sharply in 2024, with researchers documenting one of the largest nationwide drops in decades. Major cities have reported significant reductions not only in murders, but also in robberies, burglaries and auto thefts. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" target="_blank" >Chicago</a> is part of that story. So are <a class="Link" href="https://www.baltimorecity.gov/mayor/news-media/press-releases/2025-01-08-mayor-scott-city-of-baltimore-mark-historic-violence-reductions" target="_blank" >Baltimore</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.tapinto.net/towns/newark/sections/law-and-justice/articles/violent-crime-falls-murders-hit-72-year-low-in-newark-despite-high-profile-shootings" target="_blank" >Newark</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://atlantaregional.org/news/uncategorized/through-the-roof-or-through-the-floor-violent-crime-in-atlanta-2024-edition/" target="_blank" >Atlanta</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.clevelandohio.gov/sites/clevelandohio/files/health/health/health_statistics/2024%20Annual%20Violence%20%26%20Injury%20Report.pdf" target="_blank" >Cleveland</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wvtm13.com/article/birmingham-police-third-quarter-crime-update/73979112" target="_blank" >Birmingham</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://memphiscrime.org/2024-annual-report/" target="_blank" >Memphis</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c20000" name="module-c20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>What do many of these cities have in common?</p><p>They are led by Black mayors.</p><p>That fact alone does not prove causation. Public safety is shaped by countless factors, from policing strategies and economic conditions to community partnerships and violence-intervention programs.</p><p>But the fact does expose the hollowness of a narrative that has become deeply embedded in our political discourse.</p><p>When crime rises in a city led by a Black mayor, critics rush to declare the city a symbol of failure. When crime falls under that same leadership, the silence is deafening.</p><p>Chicago knows this dynamic better than most.</p><p>For years, the city has served as a political prop for those eager to paint urban America as a lawless wasteland. Donald Trump frequently invoked <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/09/30/donald-trump-pete-hegseth-chicago-military-training-ground-national-guard-operation-midway-blitz" >Chicago</a> during his campaigns and presidency as an example of what he claimed was urban collapse. More recently, his allies have continued to portray major cities as places overrun by crime and chaos, despite mounting evidence that crime trends are moving in the opposite direction.</p><p>The purpose of this rhetoric is often larger than crime itself. It reinforces a broader narrative that America's diverse cities are inherently dysfunctional and that the leaders elected by their residents are incapable of governing effectively.</p><p>The data increasingly undermine that claim.</p><p>Baltimore recently recorded one of the most <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/17/us/baltimore-historic-decline-murder-homicide.html" target="_blank" >dramatic declines</a> in homicides in its modern history. Atlanta has seen substantial reductions in murders. Chicago's violent crime trends have moved downward. Cities across the country are reporting progress that would have been difficult to imagine during the height of the pandemic-era surge in violence.</p><p>This progress did not happen by accident.</p><p>It reflects years of investment in violence-prevention initiatives, community-based intervention programs, youth engagement efforts, neighborhood revitalization and targeted law enforcement strategies. It reflects the work of clergy, outreach workers, educators, grassroots leaders, law enforcement officers and public officials. It reflects communities that refused to surrender to despair.</p><p>And yes, it reflects leadership.</p><p>I know this from experience. During my two terms as mayor of New Orleans, we achieved dramatic reductions in crime while advancing neighborhood revitalization, economic development and police reform. I also know New Orleans is not unique. Across the country, Black mayors have long demonstrated that effective leadership and smart public safety strategies can produce real results. <a class="Link" href="https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/celebrating-maynard-jackson-50-years-of-influence/" target="_blank" >Maynard Jackson</a> helped guide Atlanta through a period of extraordinary growth and modernization. <a class="Link" href="https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/honorable-wellington-webb" target="_blank" >Wellington Webb</a> presided over major crime reductions and economic expansion in Denver. <a class="Link" href="https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/honorable-kurt-schmoke" target="_blank" >Kurt Schmoke</a> brought innovative thinking to public safety and governance in Baltimore.</p><p>Time and again, Black mayors have helped make cities safer, stronger, and more prosperous through a combination of accountability, community partnership and opportunity.</p><p>Black mayors should not receive sole credit for falling crime rates. But neither should they be denied credit when their cities make measurable progress. Leadership means assembling coalitions, setting priorities, allocating resources and holding institutions accountable. The mayors leading many of America's largest cities have spent years pursuing exactly that work.</p><p>The irony is difficult to ignore. At the very moment critics continue to describe Black-led cities as uniquely dangerous, many of those cities are producing some of the nation's most encouraging public safety outcomes.</p><p>That reality deserves acknowledgment, not because the mayors are Black, but because the stereotype is.</p><p>Not every problem has been solved. Anyone who has lost a loved one to violence knows better. Too many neighborhoods still experience trauma. Too many families live with fear. Too many young people remain vulnerable to cycles of poverty and violence.</p><p>But progress matters.</p><p>If we are willing to amplify stories of failure, we must also be willing to recognize stories of success.</p><p>America's cities are proving that public safety improves when communities invest in prevention, accountability, opportunity, and partnership. Many of those success stories are unfolding under Black mayors.</p><p>For generations, political actors have tried to associate Black political leadership with urban decline while portraying predominantly white-led jurisdictions as models of competence. The evidence before us challenges those assumptions. It reminds us that effective governance cannot be measured by race, ideology or partisan affiliation. It must be measured by results, and those results are increasingly harder to ignore.</p><p>I saw firsthand in New Orleans what can happen when communities, law enforcement, civic leaders and public officials work together around a shared commitment to public safety. From my administration to today's generation of Black mayors, city leaders have shown that crime can be reduced while opportunity expands. The results speak far more loudly than the stereotypes ever could.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3c0000" name="module-3c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Does Chicago need a permanent festival site? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers whether Chicago needs a permanent festival site. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Northerly Island. The old U.S. Steel South Works site. The old Michael Reese site. Big swaths of empty land on the South and West sides."<br><i>— Michael James</i></p><p>"I love festivals in Grant Park. Why change? Lollapalooza pays upwards of a million dollars a year to fix and improve the park. They do a phenomenal job."<br><i>— Jay Boogy</i></p><p>"No, we don't need a designated event space. Having festivals in different areas of the city may be a bit of a nuisance for residents, but think of the small neighborhood businesses in the area that probably see a boost in sales in the summer."<br><i>— Cynthia Holden</i></p><p>"Milwaukee’s Summerfest grounds say, 'Hold my brat.'"<br><i>— Scott Bloom</i></p><p>"The Salt Shed is about to expand and add another 15,000-person outdoor venue across the street. They should just sign a contract with the city and become the official festival grounds. They'll have three venue spaces and plenty of space to mingle between them."<br><i>— Corey Radtke</i></p><p>"Absolutely. That is what they should have done with Northerly Island — three sides of it is water so you would only need to secure the north end."<br><i>— David Bernicky</i></p><p>"Yes. When Riot Fest, held annually in Douglass Park, was damaged by torrential rain and crowd traffic, many RFers suggested Chicago have a dedicated festival grounds like Milwaukee has for Summerfest. Take music fests out of neighborhood parks and put them in a space with direct access to parking, options for public transportation and built for a large number of attendees."<br><i>— Loretta Peterson</i></p><p>"Use the Soldier Field site once the Bears move out."<br><i>— Ty Nelson</i></p><p>"Yes. It costs a lot of money to clean and repair the aftermath of festivals, and these events disturb surrounding neighborhoods and the local wildlife. Plus, public parks should always be available to everyone, not just festival goers."<br><i>— Janice Flynn</i></p><p>"No to one permanent site. As a frequent attendee of festivals in our city, part of the joy attending festivals of all kinds is enjoying the different Chicago neighborhoods and parks. One site will mean all the events become very generic. This would mean less interest and less participation, less revenue and less getting to know all the areas of our great city. We are not Milwaukee, we have many more neighborhoods to enjoy."<br><i>— Amy Hand</i><br></p>

entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/candace-chambers" target="_blank" >Candace Dane Chambers</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>This month, the University of Chicago community has been rocked by two cases of reported sexual assault at fraternity houses. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/20/sexual-assault-university-of-chicago-uchicago-lawsuit" >One incident</a> occurred in February at Alpha Delta Phi, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/12/woman-21-sexually-assaulted-near-the-university-of-chicago-in-hyde-park" >the other</a> took place just weeks ago at the off campus Alpha Epsilon Pi house. These reports emerged in the midst of an already tense national debate about collegiate sexual violence, spurred by the recent revelation of Cornell University’s perceived mishandling of an alleged frat house gang rape in 2024.</p><p>UChicago students are now calling on administrators to improve its assault prevention and survivor support programs. At a Wednesday night rally, national advocates came together with student organizers to stand in solidarity with victims and propose new policies for a safer campus.</p><h3><b>How I got this photo:</b></h3><p>The rally began at 6 p.m., so I was shooting outdoors after sunset, which is always a struggle. Thankfully, the local TV crews were also on the scene with their large LED lights pointed at the podium. I piggybacked off their lighting to capture each speaker and any faces in the crowd that the light spilled onto. I spotted senior student Jack Huber standing on the front line of ralliers. I was initially standing directly across from him, and after capturing a few wide shots head on, I walked around the media set up to shoot from inside the crowd. I stood flush with the front line and crouched down to shoot up on Huber. Only his face and sign were lit, so I dropped my ISO and allowed all the surrounding elements to fall into shadow. entries.title: Get vaccinated to protect yourself and others
entries.summary: <p>With fall underway, it already feels like every day is busy with school activities, raking leaves and prepping for the upcoming holidays. But as we carry on with our bustling lives, we can’t forget the importance of our individual and shared responsibility to get our seasonal vaccinations.</p><p>We're already seeing an <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/video/news/local/flu-season-starts-unusually-early-this-year/4007184/" target="_blank" >early start</a> to this year’s flu season, and I’ve seen friends who were waiting to get their vaccinations get sick already. Soon as it gets cooler outside, we're going to be spending more time indoors, making it more likely for illnesses to spread.</p><p>In 2012, we saw the highest number of cases of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2014/12/24/18457024/whooping-cough-epidemic-hits-california-is-chicago-next" target="_blank" >whooping cough</a> since the 1950s, and today we are experiencing our <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/jul/24/us-measles-infections-record-high" target="_blank" >country’s largest measles outbreak</a> since 1991.</p><p>These dangerous outbreaks were and are completely preventable. They serve as a reminder of the importance of vaccinations to protect our co-workers, teachers, infants, older family members and others who may be more vulnerable.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health's new <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/illinois/iisnewsattachments/32922-091026-9-10-2026-idph-immunization-guidance.pdf.pdf" target="_blank" >immunization guidance</a> for children and adults was reviewed and approved by 20 highly qualified medical experts on the Illinois Immunization Advisory Committee. This science and fact-based guideline is our best protection against the flu and other respiratory viruses.</p><p>Getting vaccinated should not be a political issue. This is a shared effort for the health of our families, friends and communities. Let's do it for each other. Here’s to a safe and healthy holiday season ahead.</p><p><i>Rob Anderson, Naperville</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ca0000" name="module-ca0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Hope isn’t enough — get out and vote</h3><p>From where I sit in the good common-sense state of Illinois, it’s unthinkable that the Democrats won’t gain traction during the midterm elections. But how does one avoid the unthinkable? How do you prevent it from happening? Sometimes it’s as simple as thinking about it.</p><p>I was talking with another communications strategist who pointed out two possible outcomes for the midterm elections: The polls are wildly wrong, and Republicans come out in droves to maintain the status quo. Or the indications of discontent and people readying to push back against the erosion of our democracy are correct, and they reinvigorate Congress and bring in a blue wave.</p><p>I say there could also be a third “unthinkable” outcome where voter suppression, the normalization of armed uniformed agents in the streets and the fear and intimidation of people with the right to vote — but who may not have been born in this country — lead to a Democratic loss. After all, this is the administration of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/06/26/project-2025-donald-trump-civil-service-heritage-foundation-viktor-orban-democracy-marc-morial-column" target="_blank" >Project 2025</a>, which saw so many of its actions come true, and where billionaires, media consolidation deals for Donald Trump's allies and capitulation by others have all changed the dynamics of what we read, watch and hear.</p><p>Yet, I believe more people are tired of seeing human rights treated like a bauble in the hands of a mercurial tyrant. I believe some Republicans don’t feel that the current folks speak for them. I believe we’ve strayed too far from the basic decency and goodness we all want to see in the world, for our families, neighbors and institutions. I believe in optimism, but we have to keep our eyes open and our wits about us.</p><p>The unspeakable can happen if we don’t speak about it. I heard author Percival Everett paraphrase the famous quote as, "Hope without strategy is foolish."</p><p>Now is the time to recognize the threats, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/10/27/illinois-voting-trump-election-day-attorney-general-kwame-raoul" target="_blank" >plan to vote</a> and make sure your vote is counted.</p><p><i>Sylvia Ewing, Country Club Hills</i></p><h3>Is that all you got?</h3><p>It seems every televised campaign ad has a candidate saying with a great deal of bravado, “I’ll stand up to Donald Trump." Does that mean when Trump is no longer in office that they will resign? I’m old enough to remember when candidates had an actual platform to run on instead of using a hot button statement to try to get elected.</p><p><i>Thomas Pries, Orland Park</i></p><h3>Sick of seeing Grant Park trashed</h3><p>I was so happy to read that a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/10/27/chicago-ballot-2026-election-permanent-festival-site-venue" >nonbinding measure</a> regarding a permanent festival site in Chicago is on the November ballot. This has been a problem for years in many parks but especially in Grant Park — our city's "front yard." It is an embarrassment to the city to have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/09/buckingham-fountain-switched-on-for-2026-summer-season" >Buckingham Fountain</a>, the Grant Park Rose Garden and other areas around the park cordoned off for much of the summer with chain-link fences, filled with utility truck trailers, portable toilets, tents, etc.</p><p>Imagine tourists coming to our city expecting to visit our beautiful Buckingham Fountain, only to find it behind chain-link fencing and being used as a staging area for events. Chicago definitely needs a large fairground to hold events without commandeering Grant Park for most of the summer. </p><p>The sites Sara Heymann mentioned in WBEZ's Courtney Kueppers' article — The 78, Soldier Field and the former Damen Silos — would all be great options for a fairground. Northerly Island could also be expanded to include a fairground. </p><p>Grant Park should be for peace and relaxation. As Montgomery Ward said: "Here is a park given to the public ... to look out upon, a place where they can go and breathe the fresh air and look out upon the lake."</p><p><i>Michael Shawgo, Edgewater</i> </p><h3>Shout-out to forensic nurses </h3><p>All victims of violence — regardless of age, gender and background — deserve expert healthcare and support in pursuing justice. Forensic nurses deliver that specialized care and commitment.</p><p>Forensic nurses know the injuries sustained as a result of abuse and assault are more than bruises or broken bones. Guided by a foundation in trauma-informed care and understanding of the laws, they are among the first to acknowledge the emotional pain and provide the safe space for a patient to seek healing and justice.</p><p>Forensic nurses may work in emergency departments, but they are vital members of teams in many places. Through their expertise, they may work as sexual assault nurse examiners, death investigators, forensic clinical nurse specialists or legal nurses. Their specialized knowledge and approach serve those who have experienced sexual assault or abuse, intimate or interpersonal violence, elder and child maltreatment, human trafficking and accidental as well as non-accidental trauma.</p><p>It takes not only distinct skills but also a special strength to be a forensic nurse.</p><p>Forensic Nurses Week, Nov. 2-8, was established to honor the extraordinary work of these nurses who practice what was first recognized as a unique specialty in 1995.</p><p>On behalf of the Emergency Nurses Association, I celebrate and appreciate forensic nurses and sexual assault nurse examiners around the world for the care they provide to patients during scary and vulnerable moments. I encourage everyone to learn more about forensic nurses and how they serve — and need support — in your communities.</p><p><i>Dustin Bass, president, Emergency Nurses Association</i></p><h3><b>ComEd is making sure data centers pay their fair share</b></h3><p>Recently in a Sun-Times story, consumer groups suggested customers could be left paying billions for grid upgrades associated with data centers. As the electricity provider for northern Illinois, ComEd takes seriously its responsibility to protect customers from unnecessary or speculative investments. It’s inaccurate to suggest that customers are exposed to — or paying for — grid upgrades made to serve large-load customers like data centers.</p><p>The groups cited in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/22/data-centers-comed-3-billion-icc-consumer-groups-cub-illinois-households" target="_blank" >Oct. 22 article</a> compared $3.1 billion in projected grid investments with $721 million in deposits. This analysis inaccurately combines different categories of costs (transmission and distribution) and overlooks nation-leading customer protections ComEd has put in place.</p><p>Approximately half of the $3.1 billion projection is related to transmission is protected through Transmission Security Agreements created by ComEd that require large-load customers to guarantee payment for use of the transmission system, even if the project isn’t built or hit its full projected use. ComEd has secured $1.1 billion in transmission revenue guarantees. ComEd has also proposed additional safeguards to make qualifying data centers put forth additional deposits for the costs of the grid upgrades required to serve them.</p><p>The $721 million does not reflect the full scope of customer protections for distribution investments or the additional deposits still being determined for projects under development.</p><p>Every projected grid investment is not and will not automatically become a cost for households, and regulators review and approve all of our investments. Regulatory rules determine which costs must be paid by individual projects and which may be shared when broader system benefits are created.</p><p>Incomplete comparisons that create the mistaken impression that billions of dollars in costs are being shifted to Illinois households won’t help us address the real issue: Electricity supply costs have risen — and customers deserve to know why: because power supply has not been added to meet growing demand.</p><p>As electricity use grows, adding generation will be essential to both future affordability and reliability. ComEd does not own power plants and does not profit from the "supply" portion of customers’ ComEd bill — those costs are passed through to customers with no markup.</p><p>Customers need clarity, not confusion, and they should not be led to believe billions of dollars in costs are being shifted to Illinois households.</p><p><i>Kristin Munsch, vice president, Regulatory, Policy and Strategy, ComEd</i></p><h3>Campus assaults tied to universities’ failures, gender inequity</h3><p>As I write, the Sun-Times has published several articles about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/21/university-chicago-sexual-assault" >two alleged sexual assaults</a> at University of Chicago fraternity houses. Meanwhile, our country also stands in the shadows of the 2024 <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/a-gang-rape-allegation-at-cornell-highlights-how-title-ix-guides-campus-sex-assault-cases" target="_blank" >alleged gang rape</a> at Cornell University.</p><p>Local and national reporting on these cases need more perspective. I write not only as a former Northwestern University undergraduate (1967 —1970) but as a university professor for more than five decades. During my college days, frat boys often drunkenly stormed across campus on "panty raids," demanding women's undergarments. A surprising number of young women tossed fancy underwear out their dorms and sorority house windows.</p><p>With the recent assaults, many are responding as if they are new and unusual. Sadly, they've been and are much more common. They're part of the more than centurylong history of fraternities and sororities; “coming of age” traditions and the unequal place of women, combined with the complicity of sororities in the vulnerability of their members and the power of so-called "Greek" fraternities and sororities. Few emphasize that Cornell’s Jane Doe is also suing her former sorority, along with her <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/cornell-university-lawsuit-fraternity-rape-allegations/" target="_blank" >alleged assailants, their fraternity chapter and the university</a>.</p><p>Precise data on campus rape allegations is often lacking because of pressures not to report sex crimes, universities’ obsessions with reputation, the economic, social and cultural power of fraternities and their influential organizations, and the typically close relationships between local police and campus authorities.</p><p>Now, more fraternity chapters seek to be "banned" from university auspices while remaining active in their houses with even less supervision.</p><p>Gender issues are complicated. We must consider harmful, sometimes deadly hazing among men and women along with alcohol, drugs and forced sex. They are interrelated and common.</p><p>Universities fail not only by accepting the power and largesse of fraternities and sororities. Few provide attractive alternative on-campus residential opportunities. These include established co-ops but increasingly popular theme houses that span social issues and pre-professional interests from health to law and safety, social welfare and social reforms.</p><p><i>Harvey J. Graff, professor emeritus of English and history, Ohio State University, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3>CTU’s chance to put money where its mouth is</h3><p>With Mayor Brandon Johnson’s recently unveiled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/21/business-community-reaction-mayor-brandon-johnson-2027-budget-corporate-head-tax" >“fair share budget”</a> and his mentor Stacy Davis Gates' consistent reminder that it’s all about the children, perhaps a partial solution to our chronic deficit is sitting in plain sight. All current and future Chicago Teachers Union retirees should have their pension taxed as ordinary income under the state tax code. This would meet the fair share standard the mayor wants and demonstrate that Ms. Davis really means it when she says it’s all about the children.</p><p><i>Rick LaBelle, Streeterville</i></p>

entries.title: Jeffery Simmons trade: Bears GM Ryan Poles pursues 'legendary stuff' as Super Bowl chase officially begins
entries.summary: <p>This was worth the grueling wait.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> general manager Ryan Poles stepped into the job in 2022 and had no choice but to burn down the roster in the first phase of a massive rebuild. He tried to develop the flawed quarterback he inherited. Losses piled up.</p><p>But Thursday signaled the end of that arduous project when he swung big on a trade for All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. He made that move thinking the Bears can win the Super Bowl this season, and it’s the first time in his five-year tenure he’s truly been able to make a move with that mindset.</p><p>“It's a different feeling,” Poles said as he thought about the journey. “We've done a lot of good work to put ourselves in this position.</p><p>“To be in the space that you're chasing championships, whereas we were just trying to get off the ground the first couple years that I was here, I feel really good about it.”</p><p>Big trades always are fun at the time. Just ask Ryan Pace. The more important part is how they play out over years.</p><p>Poles needs this move to vault the Bears to the Super Bowl and needs to be correct that the Bears are getting Simmons at the optimal point of his career.</p><p>On the first point, they already were in the conversation for the Super Bowl, albeit on the outskirts. They’d still be an upstart looking to upend teams like the Bills, Rams, Chiefs and 49ers, as well as an underdog in their visit to the defending champion Seahawks on Monday. But attacking one of their biggest weaknesses by landing arguably the NFL’s best player at that position could put them on equal footing.</p><p>As for Simmons, while there’s risk in trading two first-round picks for a 29-year-old, he’s still squarely in his prime at that position. It’s reasonable to expect a star defensive tackle to hold up through at least his early 30s, and the Bears have him under contract through 2030.</p><p>Poles had to be incredibly confident on both fronts to pursue the trade.</p><p>He also had to be as sure as any general manager can be that his roster, especially quarterback Caleb Williams, was championship-caliber and that this was the time to go for it.</p><p>“The ‘all-in’ narrative is there, [but] from the moment we started training camp this year we were all-in,” Poles said.</p><p>After watching his patient, conservative approach and his priority of “sustainable” success, it was hard to imagine him ever giving up two first-round picks in a trade. Way outside his comfort zone. Poles had to be so convinced that he was willing to bet his job on it.</p><p>Rams general manager Les Snead famously wore a t-shirt that said, “[Expletive] them picks,” at their Super Bowl parade after he mortgaged his team’s future and came away a championship in the 2021 season. Poles referenced that unprompted Friday and clarified, “That’s really not what we’re about.”</p><p>So please stop all the memes. Snead's catchphrase is the opposite of Poles' ethos.</p><p>Poles got this job, after all, because Pace followed a similar strategy only to go 6-11 that same season. Poles has been determined to prevent the Bears from bottoming out the way they did in 2021.</p><p>If there was any position other than quarterback, though, that he believed would justify this expense, it’d be on the defensive line. And defensive tackle, in particular, has been a persistent problem.</p><p>He valued it enough to offer Larry Ogunjobi a sizable contract in 2022, even as he was in demolition mode. The Bears rescinded the offer when he failed their physical, then spent a second-round pick on Gervon Dexter in 2023. Poles went back to free agency in the 2025 offseason and spent on Grady Jarrett.</p><p>None of it revolutionized his defensive line, and Poles lamented it as he watched teams like the Seahawks, Eagles and Chiefs win championships with dominant defensive tackles.</p><p>“Super Bowl teams all have what we call a ‘red-level’ interior defensive lineman,” Poles said. “You need one.</p><p>“We’ve been searching, but sometimes the draft doesn’t provide that to you. Free agency doesn’t really [provide them]; it’s very hard for guys to get out of the building when they have all of those things that we’re talking about. [Simmons] was an opportunity that we had to jump on.”</p><p>When Poles works on trades like this in his office, he has a replica of the Lombardi Trophy the Chiefs won when he was an executive for them behind his desk. He talked to reporters wearing a navy quarter-zip with the Bears’ “1946 World Champions” logo on the chest. In <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/09/02/like-it-was-meant-to-be-bears-gm-ryan-poles-rebuild-comes-together-faster-than-he-or-anyone-imagined" >a Sun-Times interview two years ago</a>, he spoke admiringly of Theo Epstein leading the Cubs out of their championship drought and openly dreamed of doing the same for the Bears.</p><p>“If you get that right,” Poles said then, “that’s legendary stuff.”</p><p>This is him throwing his hardest punch. He’s got the coach and the quarterback, and he’s hoping Simmons’ impact will ripple through the defense. The rebuild is over. The chase is on.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Beloved niece lacks respect for relatives' time
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We live 500 miles from our nearest relatives, but a niece is attending a university about 50 miles away. We invite her to join us for holidays and weekends, and sometimes she asks to visit to escape from roommate drama.</p><p>We love having her, but she often says she's coming at one time only to arrive hours or days later. Last time, she told us she was coming on Friday afternoon and didn't show up until Sunday afternoon (she does keep us updated).</p><p>We have busy lives and often set aside our regular activities to shop for special meals or make reservations for activities to do with her. Instead, we end up sitting home because our other activities were canceled to spend time with her.</p><p>Her parents, when they travel to this area, also do this or expect us to travel to meet them within about 100 miles, but they keep changing the plans, so our schedules are disrupted. They try to cram so many things into a day that visits to a special place are often pushed to the end of the day, and we must rush through before closing.</p><p>When we visit them, they rarely alter their plans for us and seem surprised when we show up on time. Sometimes, we have to wait hours for them to come home when we agreed on our time of arrival. We love spending time with them, but this just makes us feel used. I don't know how to express this to them without alienating them. — <i>ON SCHEDULE IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR ON SCHEDULE:</b> What boorish, disrespectful relatives you have been catering to. Worse, they have passed their disregard for the feelings of others along to their daughter. You are long overdue for a conversation with that niece, informing her that if she can't show up on the agreed-upon date, she should cancel rather than leaving you hanging for two days. Make sure she understands that you won't be home if she arrives hours late.</p><p>Deliver a similar message to her parents. If you are left waiting for more than 30 minutes (and I think that's generous), you will carry on without them or go home.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a 7-year-old daughter who hasn't seen her dad in years. Her own father wants nothing to do with her. He has always hidden our child from his family and tries to keep us a secret. I'm getting sick and tired of this behavior, and the department of child support can't do anything because he ignores their calls. What can I do? Is it best to move on and cut off contact for good since he's not interested in our daughter? — <i>DONE WITH NON-DAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR DONE:</b> Sadly, you can't force a deadbeat dad to have a relationship with his daughter. You would be justified in cutting him out of your life completely. I must ask, though: Have you consulted a lawyer about any of this? Even if he's unwilling to be present as a parent, a father is legally required to provide financial support in most cases.</p><p><b>DEAR READERS:</b> It's Halloween, a time for fun and fantasy! I hope that any celebrating you do tonight will be creative, fun and safe for everyone involved. Happy Halloween!</p><p>And a reminder that daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. Sunday. Don't forget to turn your clocks back one hour at bedtime tonight. And while you're at it, be sure to put fresh batteries in your fire alarms and smoke detectors. — <i>LOVE, ABBY</i></p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i> </p>

entries.title: Seahawks boast the NFL's best receiver — the Bears must 'just try to contain him'
entries.summary: <p>Of all the things the Seahawks’ Jaxon Smith-Njigba has done to become the best wide receiver in the NFL, one stands out to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> receiver Rome Odunze.</p><p>Smith-Njigba’s body stays in the same position, whether he’s about to run a slant, a corner route or a fly route. That makes it hard, if not impossible, for cornerbacks to guess which route he’s running.</p><p>‘‘A lot of people right now are talking about his posture in his routes and how he doesn’t give any indicators, and it’s very true,’’ Odunze told the Sun-Times. ‘‘When you can keep that pad level through all those routes and accelerations, it’s hard to gauge what you’re doing.’’</p><p>It’s artful, sure, but it’s also physically demanding.</p><p>‘‘It takes a lot of strength,’’ Odunze said.</p><p>It will take even more strength for the Bears to stop him Monday. A secondary that has struggled this season — veteran Jaylon Johnson has given up a whopping 113.1 passer rating on balls thrown in his direction — is facing its toughest cover of the season. Consider:</p><p>• Smith-Njigba leads the NFL with 867 receiving yards and eight receiving touchdowns. Nobody in the Super Bowl era has had more than 850 receiving yards and eight receiving scores through seven games.</p><p>• He’s on pace to finish the season with 2,106 receiving yards, which would be the most in NFL history by 142 yards.</p><p>• He has posted at least 100 receiving yards in all but one game so far this season. If he does it again Monday, he’ll be only the fifth receiver in NFL history to hit triple digits in seven of his first eight games in a season.</p><p>‘‘That’s kind of the engine that gets [the Seahawks’ offense] going,’’ Bears coach Ben Johnson said.</p><p>Smith-Njigba is targeted on his routes — and on the highest percentage of his team’s passes — more than any receiver in the game.</p><p>‘‘You try to do what you can to stop him, but it’s a part of the game,’’ Bears safety Cam Lewis said. ‘‘You just can’t give up big plays. . . . Just try to contain him. Just try not to look up and see he has [freaking] five catches for a buck-fifty.’’</p><p>Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen was quick to rattle off the traits that concern him — Smith-Njigba’s ability to beat press coverage at the line of scrimmage, to create space at the top of his route and having a knack for winning contested catches — before settling on what makes him exceptional: Smith-Njigba’s 274 yards after catch ranks third among receivers.</p><p>The Seahawks were trailing the Patriots by seven points in the fourth quarter of their game in Week 1 when, on fourth-and-one, they threw a hitch pass to Smith-Njigba. He caught the ball at the Patriots’ 41 and knifed his way up the field, being touched only once, before tying the score.</p><p>‘‘He can take a short throw, and it’s 40 or 50 yards later before somebody is finally getting him down on the ground,’’ Allen said.</p><p>That’s particularly concerning to a secondary that couldn’t tackle Patriots running back Rhamondre Stevenson on a 48-yard touchdown at the end of the first half Oct. 22. Jaylon Johnson was the only player to touch Stevenson, but he just grazed his undershirt.</p><p>Allen acknowledged Johnson’s inconsistency, saying Johnson ‘‘would say himself there’s some things that he has to improve on.’’ The entire secondary could say the same about that touchdown by the Patriots.</p><p>‘‘That was a bad play by the defense,’’ safety Dillon Thieneman said. ‘‘It wasn’t who we are, but we definitely need to learn from it.’’</p><p>The Bears bottling up Smith-Njigba would</p>
